aAbout: Argos Atlas is a hosted real-time world map that aggregates already-open official feeds — above all public cameras, which it claims number over 200,000 from official portals in more than 190 countries — and paints everything that moves around them on one flat map: flights, ships, war frontlines, verified events, infrastructure, earthquakes, fires and prediction markets. The live map is free with a free account; ARGOS PRO adds recording, history, an AI analyst layer and a 3D globe mode.
aStrengths: Argos Atlas is the deeper working atlas for the present tense: an order of magnitude more cameras (its claim), camera recording with a 24-hour scrubbable archive, flight and ship history (7–90 days), sanctions and dark-vessel flags, verified frontlines and events, geofence alerts and a 16-camera videowall. It asks nothing of your computer — a free account in any browser — and its team plans (up to 10 seats on DIVISION) aim it at newsrooms and analysts, not just the curious.
bAbout: Google Earth is the world's most detailed free virtual globe: high-resolution satellite and aerial imagery, 3D cities and terrain, Street View at ground level, a historical-imagery archive reaching back decades, and tools for measuring, drawing and telling stories with places (including guided Voyager tours and Google Earth Studio for animations). Google Earth Pro — once $399/year — has been free since 2015. Everything in it is archival: the imagery shows the world as it was photographed, not as it is now.
bStrengths: Google Earth is the gold standard for exploring a place: the most detailed 3D cities anywhere, Street View, the deepest historical imagery archive (decades back), powerful measurement and drawing tools, KML/KMZ data import and Earth Studio for cinematic animations — all permanently free. Nobody matches its imagery depth, 3D building coverage and the familiarity billions of users already have.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. Argos Atlas is a hosted live atlas built around camera scale (200,000+ claimed), live flights and ships, recording, history and verification layers, free to open with an account and paid to remember. Google Earth is a free 3D globe built around place — the deepest satellite and aerial archive, 3D cities and Street View — with no live data at all. If you want to monitor the planet now, open Argos Atlas; if you want to explore a place in 3D and through time, open Google Earth.

intro: Argos Atlas and Google Earth both put the whole planet on one screen — and they mean opposite things by it. Argos Atlas is a hosted live atlas: a flat map claiming 200,000+ public cameras, with live flights, ships, frontlines, verified events and prediction markets layered around them, free with a free account. Google Earth is Google's free virtual globe: the deepest archive of satellite and aerial imagery ever assembled, with 3D cities, Street View and decades of historical imagery. One shows the world as it is moving now; the other shows it as it was photographed.
pricingA: The live atlas is free and, in Argos's words, 'will stay free' — it asks for a free account and shows ads with camera limits. ARGOS PRO (EUR, VAT included in the EU/UK) lists OUTPOST at €15.99/month or €44.99 for 12 months, DISTRICT at €56.99/month or €134.99 for 12 months, DIVISION at €199/month or €809 for 12 months, and AGENCY at €1,049.99/month for registered companies. First-month welcome discounts apply to OUTPOST and DISTRICT; there is no free trial.
pricingB: Completely free — Google Earth Pro (once $399/year) has been free since 2015. No paid tiers, no subscriptions; a Google account is optional, needed only for saving places and projects.

verdictA: Choose Argos Atlas if you want a ready-to-open working map with the biggest claimed camera catalogue, live flights and ships, recording, history and alerts — and you're willing to pay for the memory features.
verdictB: Choose Google Earth if you explore places — checking a neighbourhood, a coastline or a construction site, walking streets in 3D, measuring land, or watching a familiar place change across decades of imagery — free, with no account required.
verdictLine: Argos Atlas is the live wire — a hosted camera-first atlas for what is happening now. Google Earth is the archive — a free photoreal 3D globe for what places look like and how they changed. One records the present; the other preserves the past in unmatched detail.
worldEye: If Argos's account wall and ads are the friction there, and Google Earth's imagery being archival is the limit there, WorldEye is the middle path: a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries, live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. It doesn't record cameras like Argos or match Google Earth's 3D cities, Street View or decades-deep archive, and its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) buys an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds rather than camera archives.
